reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use at 15.0% in its latest reading for Other services, NAICS 81, the grouping that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, up from 13.7% in the prior period. The question behind that number is narrow and behavioral: in the last two weeks, did this business use AI. It is a firm-level measure for a broad services grouping rather than a nonprofit-specific count, so it should be read as the closest official baseline available rather than a precise sector rate. The Census series has asked the question since September 2023, which makes trend comparison possible going forward.

On what the technology is actually used for, Candid, the nonprofit data organization behind GuideStar and Foundation Center, points to the donor-facing side: donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities, which means many won't ever see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter. That reframes adoption as partly a discovery problem rather than only an internal efficiency question. The Center for Effective Philanthropy examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications, and NTEN, the Nonprofit Technology Network, runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits.

The access side of the picture comes from The AI Equity Project, which describes structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs intended to make AI accessible, ethical, and practical for all communities. It turns public libraries and community spaces into interactive learning environments, brings senior citizens and student volunteers together around practical AI tools, and operates as a global network providing standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities. Its International AI for Impact Challenge invites engineering candidates to pitch operational algorithms, with top participants securing engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advisement. NTEN frames the same terrain as a matter of inequity, stating that nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector that must be dismantled, and it offers scholarships, an equity guide, and recognition of open source tools built for nonprofit and advocacy use.

Where money and organizations concentrate is only partly visible in this material. Candid tracks grantmaking trends, including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure. This site's own catalogue of nonprofits and open source foundations lists four individually verified organizations: LMSYS, which stewards Chatbot Arena as shared evaluation infrastructure outside the commercial incentives of the labs being evaluated, Khan Academy as an end user of AI capability in education, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation as stewards of creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. That page is explicit about its limits: there are no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights, and the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

On risk and regulation the harvested material is thin, and it is better to say so than to extrapolate. NTEN's research covers AI policy adoption among nonprofits and its framing centers equity in technology use, funding, and creation. This site's classification work emphasizes auditability, recording the document each organization published about itself and the date that source was last read, on the reasoning that a classification keeping no evidence cannot be audited. Beyond that, the sources here do not describe a regulatory posture specific to nonprofits.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the practical takeaways are modest and grounded. The Census Bureau gives a measured baseline rather than an anecdote, at 15.0% for the broader services grouping. Candid's finding suggests that donor research behavior is already shifting whether or not an organization adopts anything internally. NTEN and The AI Equity Project both treat capability and equity as the binding constraints, and this site's coverage of the sector frames the work as grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets, with governance capacity as the constraint. Stanford HAI's annual AI Index is cited here as the citable macro series on AI's social impact and implementation across mission-driven and public-sector organizations, though no figures from it appear in this material.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues four individually verified organisations ,  two nonprofits and two open-source foundations ,  each carrying a sourced classification note, the source that decided it, and the date that source was last read. It identifies LMSYS as the most directly AI-central entry, stewarding Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the wider AI community uses to benchmark model quality, and describes Khan Academy as an end-user of AI capability in education rather than a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation are said to steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, though their primary missions predate AI and are not defined by it. The page also sets out what it does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights, with the notes confirming only organisational structure and nonprofit status rather than funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
